GDPR Article: Art. 5(1) Principles Relating to Processing and Art. 5(2) Accountability
rationale: Art. 5 sets the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and 5(2) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance with them. Data Privacy Compliance provides the demonstrable accountability and oversight that proves the organization meets those principles.

GDPR Article: Art. 5(1)(c) Data Minimisation and Art. 5(1)(e) Storage Limitation
rationale: Personal data must be limited to what is necessary and kept in identifiable form no longer than needed. Classification & Handling applies sensitivity-based handling rules, retention schedules and secure deletion to personal data.

GDPR Article: Art. 5(1)(d) Accuracy and Art. 16 Right to Rectification
rationale: Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date, and data subjects may require inaccurate data to be rectified without undue delay. Privacy Controls embeds the record-correction and rights-handling capability that fulfils those obligations.

GDPR Article: Art. 6 Lawfulness of Processing and Art. 7 Conditions for Consent
rationale: Processing is lawful only on one of the Art. 6(1) bases, and consent must be demonstrable, specific and withdrawable. Data Privacy Compliance requires the lawful basis for each processing activity to be identified and documented before collection, with consent records retained.

GDPR Article: Art. 6 Lawfulness of Processing and Art. 24 Responsibility of the Controller
rationale: Art. 24 requires the controller to implement appropriate data protection policies and measures and to be able to demonstrate compliance. Privacy Policies defines the rules for lawful, fair and transparent processing that those measures enforce.

GDPR Article: Art. 9 Special Categories of Personal Data and Art. 10 Criminal Conviction Data
rationale: Processing of special category and criminal offence data is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) condition applies, and such data requires heightened protection. Classification & Handling classifies these categories at the highest sensitivity and enforces stricter handling and access rules.

GDPR Article: Art. 12 Transparent Information and Art. 13 and 14 Information to be Provided
rationale: Controllers must provide concise, intelligible information about processing at the point of collection or within one month of indirect collection. Transparency governs the creation, approval and publication of privacy notices and AI-use disclosures that meet those content requirements.

GDPR Article: Art. 15 Right of Access
rationale: Data subjects may obtain confirmation of processing, a copy of their personal data and the supplementary information in Art. 15(1), normally within one month. Privacy Controls implements the data subject request handling that locates and produces that data.

GDPR Article: Art. 17 Right to Erasure and Art. 19 Notification Obligation
rationale: Controllers must erase personal data without undue delay when an Art. 17(1) ground applies and inform recipients of erasure or rectification. Privacy Controls provides the deletion workflow and recipient notification, with evidence of destruction.

GDPR Article: Art. 18 Right to Restriction and Art. 21 Right to Object
rationale: Data subjects may require processing to be restricted while a dispute is resolved and may object to processing based on legitimate interests or for direct marketing. Privacy Controls provides the technical capability to freeze records and maintain suppression lists.

GDPR Article: Art. 20 Right to Data Portability
rationale: Data subjects may receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller. Privacy Controls implements the export capability that satisfies the right.

GDPR Article: Art. 22 Automated Individual Decision-Making
rationale: Data subjects have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects, and where such processing is allowed the controller must provide human intervention and the ability to contest the decision. Accountability ensures every AI decision has a traceable human owner with authority to intervene and act.

GDPR Article: Art. 22 Automated Individual Decision-Making with Art. 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 15(1)(h) Meaningful Information about the Logic Involved
rationale: Where automated decision-making is used, the controller must give meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and consequences for the data subject. Explainability provides audience-appropriate interpretability and disclosure of model logic and limits.

GDPR Article: Art. 25 Data Protection by Design and by Default
rationale: Controllers must implement measures such as pseudonymisation and data minimisation into processing by design, and by default process only the personal data necessary for each purpose. Privacy Controls embeds privacy-enhancing technologies and governance in all systems.

GDPR Article: Art. 25 Data Protection by Design and by Default
rationale: Privacy by design requires privacy measures to be determined at the time the means of processing are decided. The Software Development Lifecycle embeds privacy checks and minimisation into design and build gates so Art. 25 is met before release.

GDPR Article: Art. 26 Joint Controllers
rationale: Joint controllers must determine their respective responsibilities in a transparent arrangement and make its essence available to data subjects. Third-Party Risk Management negotiates and tracks that allocation of responsibilities in the contract.

GDPR Article: Art. 28 Processor and Art. 29 Processing under Authority of the Controller
rationale: Controllers may use only processors providing sufficient guarantees, under a contract containing the Art. 28(3) terms including audit rights and sub-processor controls. Third-Party Risk Management performs the due diligence and contracting that produce and monitor those data processing agreements.

GDPR Article: Art. 30 Records of Processing Activities
rationale: Controllers and processors must maintain records of processing activities covering purposes, categories of data and recipients, transfers, retention periods and security measures. Data Mapping documents end-to-end data flows for collection, processing, storage, sharing, retention and deletion, which is the content of the record.

GDPR Article: Art. 30 Records of Processing Activities (AI training and inference data)
rationale: Where personal data is used to train or operate AI systems, the record of processing must cover those datasets and purposes. Datasets & Tagging labels datasets by provenance, purpose, licence and sensitivity so AI processing can be recorded accurately.

GDPR Article: Art. 31 Cooperation with the Supervisory Authority and Art. 24 Responsibility of the Controller
rationale: Controllers and processors must cooperate with the supervisory authority on request and implement appropriate measures to demonstrate compliance. The Privacy Program establishes the enterprise-wide privacy management program that owns that accountability and the authority relationship.

GDPR Article: Art. 32 Security of Processing
rationale: Art. 32 requires technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality and resilience of systems and to restrict access to personal data. Identity Management enforces authenticated, least-privilege access to systems and datasets containing personal data.

GDPR Article: Art. 32(1)(a) Pseudonymisation and Encryption
rationale: Art. 32 names pseudonymisation and encryption as measures appropriate to the risk. Cryptographic Management governs the approved algorithms and key management that implement encryption of personal data at rest and in transit.

GDPR Article: Art. 32(1)(b) and (c) Resilience and Restoration of Availability
rationale: Controllers must ensure the ongoing availability and resilience of processing systems and the ability to restore availability and access to personal data in a timely manner after an incident. Resilience Controls engineers systems to resist, absorb and recover from disruptive events.

GDPR Article: Art. 32(1)(d) Regular Testing and Evaluation of Measures
rationale: Art. 32 requires a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of security measures. Verification confirms that implemented controls operate as designed and meet policy requirements.

GDPR Article: Art. 33 Notification of a Personal Data Breach to the Supervisory Authority
rationale: Controllers must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach unless it is unlikely to result in a risk, and processors must notify the controller without undue delay. Incident Response: Privacy manages the assessment of personal data breaches and drives the response within that window.

GDPR Article: Art. 33 Notification to the Supervisory Authority
rationale: The notification must contain the Art. 33(3) elements and all breaches must be documented. Regulatory Reporting meets the content and timing requirements of regulatory breach reporting.

GDPR Article: Art. 34 Communication of a Personal Data Breach to the Data Subject
rationale: Where a breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, the controller must communicate it to them without undue delay in clear and plain language. Privacy Notification Requirements notifies affected individuals per legal obligation after a verified breach.

GDPR Article: Art. 35 Data Protection Impact Assessment and Art. 36 Prior Consultation
rationale: A DPIA is required before processing likely to result in high risk, including systematic evaluation based on automated processing, and the authority must be consulted where residual risk remains high. AI Impacts identifies potential impacts of AI processing on individuals and integrates mitigations, which is the assessment Art. 35 requires for AI-driven processing.

GDPR Article: Art. 35 Data Protection Impact Assessment
rationale: DPIAs must be carried out and documented as part of day-to-day privacy operations, with advice sought from the DPO. The Privacy Program (MANAGE) operationalizes the DPIA process for all high-risk processing, not only AI.

GDPR Article: Art. 37 Designation, Art. 38 Position and Art. 39 Tasks of the Data Protection Officer
rationale: Where required, a DPO must be designated, involved properly and in a timely manner in all data protection matters, protected from dismissal for performing the role and tasked with monitoring compliance, advising on DPIAs and liaising with the authority. The Privacy Oversight Committee provides the oversight structure and decision authority within which the DPO operates independently. Partial alignment: the DPO is an individual role; the committee provides its reporting line and independence.

GDPR Article: Art. 39 Tasks of the Data Protection Officer
rationale: The DPO must monitor compliance with the GDPR and with the controller's policies, including awareness-raising and training of staff. Data Privacy Compliance provides the compliance monitoring and accountability that the DPO's tasks oversee.

GDPR Article: Art. 44 General Principle for Transfers and Art. 45 Adequacy Decisions
rationale: Transfers of personal data to third countries are allowed only under Chapter V conditions. Data Mapping documents where personal data is stored and transferred, including cross-border flows, so each transfer can be matched to a lawful mechanism.

GDPR Article: Art. 46 Transfers Subject to Appropriate Safeguards
rationale: Absent an adequacy decision, transfers require appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules. Third-Party Risk Management puts those safeguards into vendor and partner contracts and tracks them.

GDPR Article: Art. 44 to 46 International Transfers in the Supply Chain
rationale: Cloud, software and model suppliers that process personal data outside the EEA create transfer risk. Supply Chain Risk identifies supplier data locations and sub-processor chains so Chapter V conditions are applied.

GDPR Article: Art. 77 Right to Lodge a Complaint and Art. 38(4) Contacting the DPO
rationale: Data subjects may contact the DPO about processing of their data and may lodge complaints with a supervisory authority. Reporting Channels provides accessible, responsive routes for individuals to raise privacy concerns before they escalate.
